¶
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Felicity'', ''Blessedness'', etc. (see ''happiness''), transport, rapture, ecstasy, blissfulness.}}

'''blissful''' (blis′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''blisful''; < ''bliss'' + ''-ful''.] '''1.''' Full of, abounding in, enjoying, or conferring bliss; full of felicity: as, “''blissful'' joy,” ''Spenser'', F. Q.; “''blissful'' solitude,” ''Milton'', P. L., iii. 69.
{{smaller block|The ''blissful'' shore of rural ease.
{{right|''Thomson'', Liberty, v.}}
Ever as those ''blissful'' creatures do I fare.
{{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}
'''2†.''' [Cf. ''blessful''.] Blessed; holy.

'''blissfully''' (blis′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''blissfuliche'', etc., < ''blisful'' + ''-liche'', -ly<sup>2</sup>.] In a blissful manner; happily.

'''blissfulness''' (blis′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''blisfulnes'', ''-nesse'', < ''blisful'' + ''-nes'', -ness.] The state or quality of being blissful; exalted happiness; supreme felicity; fullness of joy.
{{smaller block|God is all-sufficient and incapable of admitting any accession to his perfect ''blissfulness''. ''Barrow'', Works, I. viii.}}

'''Blissinæ''' (bli-sī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Blissus'' + ''-inæ''.] A subfamily of heteropterous insects, of the family ''Lygæidæ'', typified by the genus ''Blissus''. See cut under ''chinch-bug''.

'''blissless''' (blis′les), ''a.'' [< ''bliss'' + ''-less''.] Destitute of bliss; wretched; hapless: as, “my ''blissless'' lot,” ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.

'''blissom''' (blis′um), ''a.'' [< Icel. ''blæsma'', in heat (said of a ewe or goat), = OD. ''blesme''.] In heat, as a ewe. [Prov. Eng.]

'''blissom''' (blis′um), ''v.'' [< ''blissom'', ''a.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To couple with a ewe: said of a ram.

thing applied to the skin to raise a blister, as a plaster of Spanish flies, mustard, etc., as a means of counter-irritation; a vesicatory.—'''4.''' In castings of different materials, an effect caused by the presence of confined bubbles of air or gas.—'''5.''' ¶
'''blister''' (blis′tėr), ''v.'' [< ''blister'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To raise a blister or blisters on, as by a burn, medical application, or friction: as, to ''blister'' one’s hands.—'''2.''' To raise filmy vesicles on by heat: as, too high a temperature will ''blister'' paint; ''blistered'' steel. See ''blister-steel.''—'''3.''' Figuratively, to cause to suffer as if from blisters; subject to burning shame or disgrace.
{{smaller block|<poem>Look, here comes one: a gentlewoman of mine,
Who, falling in the flaws of her own youth,
Hath ''blister’d'' her report. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 3.}}</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To rise in blisters, or become blistered.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I prove honey-mouth’d, let my tongue ''blister.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 2.}}
<poem>The house walls seemed
''Blistering'' in the sun, without a tree or vine
To cast the tremulous shadow of its leaves.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Prel. to Among the Hills.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|blinkard|589|blithesome}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|In some parts we see many glorious and eminent stars, in others few of any remarkable greatness, and, in some, none but ''blinkards'' and obscure ones.
{{right|''Hakewill'', Apology, p. 237.}}}}
'''3.''' One who lacks intellectual perception.   ''Skelton.''—'''4.''' One who wilfully shuts his eyes to what is happening; one who blinks facts. [Sometimes used attributively.]

'''blink-beer''' (blingk′bēr), ''n.''   [< ''blink'', ''v.'', I., 6, + ''beer''.]   Beer kept unbroached till it is sharp.

'''blinker''' (bling′kėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who blinks.—'''2.''' One of two leather flaps placed on the sides of a horse’s head to prevent him from seeing sidewise or backward; a blind or blinder; hence, figuratively, any obstruction to sight or discernment.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor bigots who but one way see,
Through ''blinkers'' of authority.</poem>
{{right|''M. Green'', The Grotto.}}}}
{{smaller block|Horses splashed to their very ''blinkers''. {{right|''Dickens.''}}}}

'''blink-eyed''' (blingk′īd), ''a.'' Having blinking or winking eyes.
{{smaller block|The foolish ''blink-eyed'' boy. {{right|''Gascoigne'', Hearbes.}}}}

'''blinking''' (bling′king), ''n.'' In ''sporting'', the fault in dogs of leaving the game as soon as it is found.
{{smaller block|The vice of ''blinking'' has been caused by over-severity in punishment for chasing poultry, etc.
{{right|''Dogs of Great Britain and America'', p. 240.}}}}

'''blinking-chickweed''' (bling′king-chik′wēd), ''n.'' The ''Montia fontana'', a small marsh-herb, natural order ''Portulacaceæ'': so called from its small half-closed flowers looking out from the axils of the leaves. Also called ''blinks''.

'''blinkingly''' (bling′king-li), ''adv.'' In a blinking or winking manner; evasively.
{{smaller block|Death, that fatal necessity which so many would overlook, or ''blinkingly'' survey, the old Egyptians held continually before their eyes.{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Mummies.}}}}

'''blinks''' (blingks), ''n.''   [< ''blink'', ''n.''; a quasi-plural form.]   Same as ''blinking-chickweed.''

'''blinky''' (bling′ki), ''a.''   [< ''blink'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Prone to blink.
{{smaller block|We were just within range, and one’s eyes became quite ''blinky'' watching for the flash from the bow.{{right|''W. H. Russell'', London Times, June 11, 1861.}}}}

'''blirt''' (blėrt), ''n.''   [A var. of ''blurt.'']   An outburst of wind, rain, or tears; specifically, ''naut.'', a gust of wind and rain. [Scotch.]

'''blirty, blirtie''' (blėr′ti), ''a.''   [< ''blirt'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Characterized by blirts or gusts of wind and rain: as, a ''blirty'' day. [Scotch.]

'''bliss''' (blis), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blis'', ''blisse'', < AS. ''blis'', ''bliss'', contr. of the unusual ''blīds'', ''blīths'' (= OS. ''blīdsea'', ''blītzea'', ''blīzza''), joy, < ''blīthe'', joyful, blithe: see ''blithe'', and cf. ''bless''<sup>1</sup>, with which the word has been notionally associated.]   '''1.''' Blitheness; gladness; lightness of heart.—'''2.''' The highest degree of happiness, especially spiritual joy; perfect felicity; supreme delight; blessedness: often, specifically, the joy of heaven.
{{smaller block|<poem>How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown,
Within whose circuit is Elysium,
And all that poets feign of ''bliss'' and joy.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|All my redeem’d may dwell in joy and ''bliss.''{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 43.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Felicity'', ''Blessedness'', etc. (see ''happiness''), transport, rapture, ecstasy, blissfulness.}}

'''blissful''' (blis′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''blisful''; < ''bliss'' + ''-ful''.]   '''1.''' Full of, abounding in, enjoying, or conferring bliss; full of felicity: as, “''blissful'' joy,” ''Spenser'', F. Q.; “''blissful'' solitude,” ''Milton'', P. L., iii. 69.
{{smaller block|The ''blissful'' shore of rural ease.
{{right|''Thomson'', Liberty, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ever as those ''blissful'' creatures do I fare.
{{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}
'''2†.''' [Cf. ''blessful''.] Blessed; holy.

'''blissfully''' (blis′fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''blissfuliche'', etc., < ''blisful'' + ''-liche'', -ly<sup>2</sup>.]   In a blissful manner; happily.

'''blissfulness''' (blis′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blisfulnes'', ''-nesse'', < ''blisful'' + ''-nes'', -ness.]   The state or quality of being blissful; exalted happiness; supreme felicity; fullness of joy.
{{smaller block|God is all-sufficient and incapable of admitting any accession to his perfect ''blissfulness''.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, I. viii.}}}}

'''Blissinæ''' (bli-sī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Blissus'' + ''-inæ''.]   A subfamily of heteropterous insects, of the family ''Lygæidæ'', typified by the genus ''Blissus''. See cut under ''chinch-bug''.

'''blissless''' (blis′les), ''a.''   [< ''bliss'' + ''-less''.]   Destitute of bliss; wretched; hapless: as, “my ''blissless'' lot,” ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.

'''blissom''' (blis′um), ''a.''   [< Icel. ''blæsma'', in heat (said of a ewe or goat), = OD. ''blesme''.]   In heat, as a ewe. [Prov. Eng.]

'''blissom''' (blis′um), ''v.''   [< ''blissom'', ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To couple with a ewe: said of a ram. II. ''intrans.'' To be in heat, as a ewe. [Prov. Eng.]

'''Blissus''' (blis′us), ''n.''   [NL.]   A genus of heteropterous insects, the type of the subfamily ''Blissinæ''. ''B. leucopterus'' is the common chinch-bug. See cut under ''chinch-bug''.

'''blist†.''' Obsolete preterit of ''bless''<sup>1</sup> and ''bless''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>And with his club him all about so ''blist'',
That he which way to turne him scarcely wist.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. viii. 13.}}}}

'''blister''' (blis′tėr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''blyster'', ''bluster''; < ME. ''blister'', and perhaps *''blyster'', < AS. *''blȳster'' = MD. ''bluyster'', a blister (but the AS. form is not found, and the ME. may be taken from OF. ''blestre'', ''blostre'', a swelling (cf. ''bloustre'', ''bloutre'', ''blotte'', a clod, ''blosse'', a swelling due to a bruise), of MD. or Scand. origin); cf. Icel. ''blástr'', a swelling (in the medical sense), lit. a blast, a blowing, = AS. ''blǣst'', a blowing, blast; cf. ''blǣdre'', a blister, bladder, etc., D. ''blaas'', G. ''blase'', a blister, etc., E. dial. ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', a pimple, etc.; ult. from the root of AS. ''blāwan'', etc., blow: see ''bladder'', ''blast'', ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, ''blow''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A thin vesicle on the skin, containing watery matter or serum, whether occasioned by a burn or other injury, by a vesicatory, or by disease; a pustule. {{smaller|It is formed (''a'') by disintegration and effusion of serum into some of the softer epidermal layers, or (''b'') by an effusion of serum between the epidermis and corium.}}

'''2.''' An elevation made by the lifting up of an external film or skin by confined air or fluid, as on plants, or by the swelling of the substance at the surface, as on steel.—'''3.''' Something applied to the skin to raise a blister, as a plaster of Spanish flies, mustard, etc., as a means of counter-irritation; a vesicatory.—'''4.''' In castings of different materials, an effect caused by the presence of confined bubbles of air or gas.—'''5.''' A distortion of peach-leaves caused by the fungus ''Exoascus deformans''; bladder-blight. See ''Exoascus.'' Also called ''blistering.''—{{smaller|'''Flying blister,''' a blister applied for a time too short to cause vesication.}}

'''blister''' (blis′tėr), ''v.''   [< ''blister'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To raise a blister or blisters on, as by a burn, medical application, or friction: as, to ''blister'' one’s hands.—'''2.''' To raise filmy vesicles on by heat: as, too high a temperature will ''blister'' paint; ''blistered'' steel. See ''blister-steel.''—'''3.''' Figuratively, to cause to suffer as if from blisters; subject to burning shame or disgrace.
{{smaller block|<poem>Look, here comes one: a gentlewoman of mine,
Who, falling in the flaws of her own youth,
Hath ''blister’d'' her report. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 3.}}</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To rise in blisters, or become blistered.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I prove honey-mouth’d, let my tongue ''blister.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The house walls seemed
''Blistering'' in the sun, without a tree or vine
To cast the tremulous shadow of its leaves.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Prel. to Among the Hills.}}}}

'''blister-beetle''' (blis′tėr-bē″tl), ''n.'' A popular name of beetles of the family ''Meloidæ'', derived from the peculiar poison (cantharidin) which is contained in their tissues. {{img float|file=century v01 p0615 c2f1.png|width=195px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Ash-gray Blister-beetle (''Macrobasis cinerea''). (Vertical line shows natural size.) ''a'', ''b'', male and female antennæ, enlarged.}} {{smaller|This poison, when brought into contact with the skin, produces blisters, and on account of this vesicatory property the dried beetles are largely used in medicine. In their earlier states the blister-beetles are parasitic on grasshopper-eggs or in the cells of mason-bees. The imagos of many American species are often very injurious to field- and garden-crops. The development of the larva, which assumes successively several forms, is very remarkable. See ''hypermetamorphosis'' and ''Epicauta''.}}}}

'''blistered''' (blis′tėrd), ''p. a.'' Having the disease called blister. See ''blister'', ''n.'', 5.

'''blister-fly''' (blis′tėr-flī), ''n.'' A beetle, also known as the Spanish fly, used in blistering; one of the blister-beetles. See ''Cantharis''.

'''blistering''' (blis′tėr-ing), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Causing or tending to cause blisters.—'''Blistering fly.''' {{smaller|Same as ''blister-fly''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' Same as ''blister'', 5.

'''blister-plaster''' (blis′tėr-plȧs″tėr), ''n.'' A plaster of Spanish flies, designed to raise a blister.

'''blister-steel''' (blis′tėr-stēl), ''n.'' Steel made by the carburization of bar-iron in a converting-furnace, the iron being heated in contact with charcoal. See ''cementation''. {{smaller|After the conversion}} into steel, the bars become covered with blisters, some not {{smaller|larger than peas, others as much as an inch in diameter. According to Percy, these blisters are probably due to the reduction of a part of the protoxid of iron existing in the mass in the form of a silicate of the protoxid, and the consequent evolution of carbonic oxid. The process is a very old one.}}

'''blistery''' (blis′tėr-i), ''a.''   [< ''blister'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Full of blisters.   ''Hooker.''

'''blit†''', ''n.'' See ''blite''<sup>2</sup>.

'''blite<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' See ''blight.''

'''blite<sup>2</sup>''' (blīt), ''n.''   [Also ''blit'' and early mod. E. ''blitte, bleit, blete''; < F. ''blette'' = Pr. ''bleda'' = Cat. ''blet'' = Sp. ''bledo,'' < L. ''blitum'': see ''Blitum.'']   A common name of several succulent-leafed plants, chiefly of the genus ''Chenopodium'' (or ''Blitum''), sometimes used as pot-herbs. {{smaller|The name is specifically given to good-King-Henry (''C. Bonus-Henricus'') and to ''Amarantus Blitum.'' The strawberry-blite, ''Chenopodium capitatum'', is so called from its red fleshy clusters of fruit. The coast-blite, ''C. maritimum'', is found in saline localities. The sea-blite, ''Suæda maritima'', is a chenopodiaceous coast-plant with nearly terete or cylindrical fleshy leaves.}}

'''blithe''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ or blīth), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''blithe, blythe,'' < AS. ''blīthe,'' joyful, glad, kind, gentle, peaceful, = OS. ''blīthi'' = OFries. *''blīde'' (in composition ''blīd-skip,'' joy), North Fries. ''blid'' = D. ''blijde, blij'' = OHG. ''blīdi,'' MHG. ''blīde'' = Icel. ''blīdhr'' = Sw. ''blid'' = Dan. ''blid'' = Goth. ''bleiths,'' merciful, kind; root uncertain: see ''bliss.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Kind; kindly. ''Levins'' (1570).—'''2.''' Glad; merry; joyous; sprightly; mirthful; gay: in colloquial use only in Scotland: as, “I’m ''blithe'' to see you.”

{{smaller block|Ful ''blithe'' . . . was every wight.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 846.}}}}
{{smaller block|No lark more ''blithe'' than he. {{right|''Bickerstaff'', Love in a Village, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hail to thee, ''blithe'' spirit!
Bird thou never wert.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Ode to a Skylark.}}}}
'''3.''' Characterized by or full of enjoyment; gladsome: said of things.
{{smaller block|O! how changed since yon ''blithe'' night! {{right|''Scott.''}}}}
{{smaller block|''Blithe'' would her brother’s acceptance be.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, x. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In June ’tis good to lie beneath a tree
While the ''blithe'' season comforts every sense.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' Cheerful, light-hearted, elated, buoyant.}}

'''II.'''† ''n.'' '''1.''' A blithe one.—'''2.''' Kindness; good will; favor.—'''3.''' Gladness; delight.

'''blithe†''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ or blīth), ''v.''   [ME. ''blīthen'' (= OHG. ''blīden'', rejoice, be blithe, = Goth. ''bleithjan, gableithjan'', be merciful, pity); from the adj.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To be blithe or merry.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make blithe; gladden.
{{smaller block|<poem>The prince of planetis that proudely is pight
Sall brace furth his bemes that oure belde ''blithes''.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 123.}}}}

'''blithe''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ or blīth), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''blithe, blythe'', < AS. ''blīthe'', adv., < ''blīthe'', a.: see ''blithe'', ''a.'']   '''1†.''' Kindly.—'''2.''' Gladly; blithely.

'''blitheful''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ′- or blīth′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''blitheful, blithful'', < ''blithe'', n., kindness, favor (= Icel. ''blīdha''), + ''-ful''.]   '''1†.''' Kindly.—'''2.''' Glad; joyous; joyful. [Poetic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The seas with ''blitheful'' western blasts
We sail’d amain.</poem>
{{right|''Greene and Lodge'', Looking Glass for Lond. and Eng.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Samuel] Lover, a versatile artist, ''blitheful'' humorist and poet. {{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 258.}}}}

'''blithely''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ′- or blīth′li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''blitheliche'', ''blethely'', ''-liche'', etc., < AS. ''blīthelīce'' (= OHG. ''blīdlīcho''), < ''blīthe'' + ''-līce'': see ''blithe'', ''a.'', and ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Kindly.—'''2.''' Gladly; joyfully; gaily.

'''blithemeat''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ′- or blīth′mēt), ''n.''   [Sc., < ''blithe'', glad, + ''meat''.]   The entertainment or refreshment provided at the birth or christening of a child. [Scotch.]

'''blithen''' (blī′ᴛ̵ʜen or -then), ''v. t.''   [< ''blithe'', ''a.'', + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''blithe'', ''v.'']   To make blithe. [Rare.]

'''blitheness''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ′- or blīth′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blithenesse'', < AS. ''blīthnes'', < ''blīthe'' + ''-nes'': see ''blithe'', ''a.'', and ''-ness''.]   The state of being blithe; gaiety; sprightliness.
{{smaller block|The delightfulness and ''blitheness'' of their [poets’] compositions.
{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', On the Soul, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Legend told of his [Eadward’s] pious simplicity, his ''blitheness'' and gentleness of mood.
{{right|''J. H. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 467.}}}}

'''blithesome''' (blīᴛ̵ʜ′- or blīth′sum), ''a.''   [< ''blithe'' + ''-some''.]   Full of blitheness or gaiety; gay; merry; cheerful; causing joy or gladness.
{{smaller block|On ''blithesome'' frolics bent.
{{right|''Thomson'', Winter.}}}}
{{smaller block|The rising sun, emerging from amidst golden and purple clouds, shed his ''blithesome'' rays on the tin weathercocks of Communipaw.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|Charmed by the spirit, alternately tender and ''blithesome'', of Procter’s songs.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 110.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
